title: Mechanical Power Transmission
summary: Power, torque and speed fundamentals, belt tension ratios, chain drives, and couplings for transmitting rotation between shafts.

sections.heading: Getting Power From A to B
sections.content:
Power transmission moves torque and speed from a driver (motor, engine) to a driven machine, usually changing the speed ratio in the process. The fundamental relation connects everything:

$$P = T \, \omega = \frac{2\pi N T}{60}$$

with $P$ in watts, $T$ in N·m, $\omega$ in rad/s, $N$ in rpm. Example — a 10 kW motor at 1440 rpm:

$$T = \frac{60 \times 10\,000}{2\pi \times 1440} = 66.3 \text{ N·m}$$

The same power at half speed needs **double the torque** — which is why speed reducers are big, and why gearbox output shafts carry much larger forces than motor shafts.

sections.heading: Belt Drives
sections.content:
Belts transmit power by **friction** between belt and pulley. The classic **Euler–Eytelwein** relation ties the tight and slack side tensions $T_1$, $T_2$ to the wrap angle $\theta$ and friction coefficient $\mu$:

$$\frac{T_1}{T_2} = e^{\mu \theta}$$

and the transmitted power is $P = (T_1 - T_2)\,v$, with $v$ the belt speed. Practical points:

- **V-belts** (wedge in groove) roughly triple the effective friction vs flat belts — the standard for industrial drives.
- **Timing (toothed) belts** transmit by positive engagement: no slip, constant ratio, used in engines and motion control.
- **Sheaves/pulleys**: minimum pulley diameter limits belt fatigue; speed ratio $i = n_1/n_2 = d_2/d_1$ (belt speed is common to both pulleys).
- **Belt speed limit**: above ~25–30 m/s centrifugal force unloads the belt from the pulley and grip collapses.
- Belt drives absorb shock and slip (torque limiting) — a feature, not always a bug, compared to positive drives.

sections.heading: Chain Drives
sections.content:
Chains transmit by **positive engagement** — no slip, higher torque density than belts, tolerant of moderate misalignment and dirty environments (the classic motorcycle/industrial drive):

- **Roller chain** (ISO 606): pitch P, roller diameter, breaking load. Speed ratio from sprocket teeth: $i = n_1/n_2 = z_2/z_1$.
- **Wear** stretches the chain (pin/bushing wear): a stretched chain climbs the sprocket teeth and skips. Lubricate properly; run a **slack span** on the drivable side.
- **Number of teeth**: minimum ~17–19 teeth for smooth running; odd tooth counts on one sprocket + even chain link count reduce resonant wear patterns.
- **Sag/tensioner**: too tight → sprocket and bearing overload; too loose → slapping and chain whip. Maintain ~2–4% of center distance as sag.
- Speed limit: roller chains get noisy and hammer above ~10 m/s; beyond that, toothed belts or gears.

Chains are a deliberate middle ground: more positive than belts, cheaper than gears, and they do not need the precise alignment gears demand.

sections.heading: Couplings & Shaft Alignment
sections.content:
Where two shaft ends must connect — motor to gearbox, gearbox to machine — a **coupling** transmits torque while accommodating **misalignment** to protect the bearings (see [[bearings-and-shafts|bearings]]):

| Coupling | Misalignment capacity | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Rigid flange | None (needs alignment) | Large torque, stiff systems |
| Jaw (spider) | Angular, parallel, axial | Cheap, damps shock; elastomer wears |
| Gear coupling | High angular/axial | Heavy industry, high torque |
| Curved-tooth gear | Highest angular | Mill drives, long spans |
| Oldham | High parallel | Light, cleanroom |
| Bellows / diaphragm | Zero backlash | Precision motion control |

Rules of thumb: keep **angular misalignment ≤ 0.5°** at couplings for long bearing life; laser-align rotating machinery (alignment is the top cause of vibration and premature bearing death); select coupling torque rating ≥ 1.5× nominal for steady drives, ≥ 2–3× for shock loads; and for **soft-start** duty consider fluid or centrifugal couplings. The coupling is a mechanical fuse — oversizing it merely moves the failure to the next-weakest element.

sections.heading: Choosing the Transmission System
sections.content:
Selection order for a real drive train:

1. **Define duty** — power, speed range, shock factor, hours/day, reversals.
2. **Final ratio** from the driven machine; split it across stages (belt + gearbox) to keep each stage reasonable.
3. **Belt** for long center distances, shock absorption, and cheap speed reduction; **chain** for positive drive in dirty environments; **gears** (see [[spur-gear-design|spur gears]]) when ratio accuracy, compactness, and high torque density rule.
4. **Coupling** the motor to the first reducer stage, sized for the starting torque and misalignment budget.
5. **Verification** — compute bearing reactions at every shaft via the transmitted torque and geometry (see [[bearings-and-shafts|bearing loads]]), then check shaft fatigue.

Efficiency tiers (typical): gears 97–99%, chains 96–98%, belts 93–97%, plus each bearing pair ~99%. At 10 kW, a 5%-inefficient drive wastes 500 W continuously — in long-running plants the efficiency choice often dominates the capital cost choice.

keyTakeaways: P = T·ω = 2πNT/60: higher reduction means higher torque on the slow shaft.
Belt grip follows T1/T2 = e^(μθ); V-belts triple friction; belts slip by design.
Chains transmit positively without gear alignment precision; watch chain stretch and sprocket skip.
Select couplings for the misalignment, not just the torque; laser-align rotating machinery.
